cases.title: The Lectures on Faith: canonized 1835, quietly removed 1921
cases.claim: In August 1835 a general assembly of the church voted to canonize the seven Lectures on Faith as the 'Doctrine' half of the Doctrine and Covenants — they are why the book is called 'Doctrine and Covenants.' They were printed as scripture for 86 years. In 1921 a committee removed them with no revelation and no vote of common consent, explaining they 'were never presented to nor accepted by the Church as being otherwise than theological lectures' — which contradicts the 1835 assembly minutes accepting the whole volume. The doctrinal driver is plain: Lecture 5 teaches the Father is 'a personage of spirit,' irreconcilable with the later D&C 130:22 doctrine that the Father has a body of flesh and bones. When the doctrine of God changed, the canon was edited to match — a de-canonization in a church that claims its canon grows only by revelation.
bom: Lectures on Faith 5 (1835 D&C: the Father 'a personage of spirit')

sources.name: Dialogue: 'The Lectures on Faith: A Case Study in Decanonization'
Church History Topics: 'Lectures on Theology (Lectures on Faith)'
Wikipedia: Lectures on Faith
MRM: 'Removing the Doctrine out of the Doctrine and Covenants'

cases.response: FAIR and Joseph Fielding Smith (a member of the 1921 committee) argue the Lectures were lessons, not revelations: they were never claimed as the word of the Lord, were incomplete on the Godhead, and were removed to avoid confusion with actual revelations. On this view 1921 was housecleaning, not de-canonization.
cases.rationale: The response concedes the key facts. The 1835 assembly voted to accept the entire book — lectures included — as 'the doctrine and covenants of their faith'; the 'never accepted as more than lessons' explanation is contradicted by the 1835 record itself. And 'incomplete on the Godhead' is a euphemism: Lecture 5's spirit-Father theology was superseded, and the canon was trimmed to match. This pairs powerfully with D&C 132 remaining in canon while disavowed: the canon is edited by administrative decision, not revelation. Conversationally clean — one question: 'What revelation removed them?' There is none.

cases.title: The prophesied temple site is owned by a church of a few thousand members
cases.claim: D&C 57 (1831) designated Independence, Missouri as the 'center place' of Zion and the spot for the temple; D&C 84 (1832) said the temple would be reared there. Not only was no temple ever built — the LDS church does not even own the dedicated spot today. The actual dedication site belongs to the Church of Christ (Temple Lot), a Hedrickite body of roughly 7,000 members worldwide that rejects Brigham Young, the endowment, and most LDS distinctives. It kept the lot through the 1890s Temple Lot litigation era and maintains a modest meetinghouse there, while the 17-million-member church whose canon prophesies that temple owns the visitors' center next door. Usage note: lead with the ownership irony, not the 'this generation' dating argument — the dating case belongs with Joseph Smith's failed prophecies and should not be double-counted here.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Temple Lot
Wikipedia: Temple Lot Case (1890s litigation)
LDS Church: 'Questions and Answers about the Temple Lot in Independence'
MRM: Church of Christ (Temple Lot)

cases.response: The church teaches the Independence temple will still be built in the Lord's timing; D&C 124:49 provides that when enemies prevent a commanded work, God no longer requires it of that generation. The church's own site Q&A affirms continued belief in a future temple in Zion and notes cordial relations with the Temple Lot church.

responseSource.name: LDS Church Q&A on the Temple Lot

cases.rationale: The D&C 124:49 escape clause cannot explain the present tense: nothing prevents the church from building in Jackson County today except that it does not own the prophesied spot and the owners will not sell — they have refused LDS offers for over a century. A 194-year-old 'center place' prophecy whose ground is held by a tiny rival restorationist church is vivid, verifiable in five minutes, and hard to spin. Graded on the ownership core, which is undisputed by all parties including the LDS church's own materials.

cases.title: Zion's Camp: the canonized promise to redeem Zion, and the canonized walk-back
cases.claim: In February 1834, D&C 103 promised the redemption of Zion (Jackson County) 'by power,' with the Lord's presence going before the armed expedition: 'the redemption of Zion must needs come by power... I will fight your battles.' Zion's Camp marched roughly 900 miles; cholera killed about a dozen members; Missouri's governor declined to help; no land was recovered. In June 1834, D&C 105 called the whole thing off — the Saints must 'wait for a little season for the redemption of Zion' — attributing the failure to the members' transgressions. Both the promise and its retraction sit in the canon today, and 192 years later the 'little season' continues: Jackson County was never redeemed. Usage note: this entry is about the canonized reversal mechanism — coordinate with the general failed-prophecies entry so the D&C 84 temple prophecy isn't counted twice.

sources.name: LDS D&C Student Manual, ch. 41 (D&C 103; 105)
BYU Religious Studies Center: 'Zion's Camp'
Doctrine and Covenants Central: Historical Context of D&C 105
Scripture Central: D&C 103-105

cases.response: Apologists read D&C 103 as conditional: D&C 105 itself explains the Saints failed to consecrate and were unprepared, so the Lord deferred rather than broke his promise. Zion's Camp is reframed as a refining trial — many future apostles and seventies were chosen from its veterans — so the expedition 'succeeded' at its real purpose.
cases.rationale: The conditionality was announced after the failure, not before it — D&C 103 reads as an unconditional promise with divine military backing ('mine angels shall go up before you'), and D&C 105 retrofits conditions once the expedition collapsed. The 'refining trial' reading concedes the stated objective failed. The unique value here is pedagogical: unlike disputed prophecy cases, the believer's own canon contains both the promise and the walk-back — no external source is needed. 'Wait for a little season' entering its third century speaks for itself.

cases.title: The 'One Mighty and Strong': a canonized prophecy that breeds prophets
cases.claim: D&C 85:7 promises that God will send 'one mighty and strong, holding the scepter of power in his hand' to 'set in order the house of God.' Because the verse is canonized and unfulfilled, it has generated a continuous stream of claimants — a Dialogue survey documents roughly eighteen principal ones, and by 1905 at least eight had already declared themselves, forcing a First Presidency statement (Deseret News, November 1905) that reinterpreted the verse as referring to Edward Partridge-era land matters and declared self-proclaimed candidates ignorant 'of God and the order of the Church.' Fundamentalist sect founders and violent figures (including the LeBaron clan) have all claimed the title. A vague canonized prophecy plus prophetic authority is a schism engine — and the institutional fix was to reinterpret the scripture by press release.

sources.name: Dialogue: 'To Set in Order the House of God: The Search for the Elusive One Mighty and Strong'
1905 First Presidency statement (B.H. Roberts records)
LDS Seminary manual on D&C 85-86
Scripture Central KnoWhy on D&C 85

cases.response: The 1905 First Presidency statement holds that the verse concerned the specific 1832 situation of Bishop Edward Partridge and land inheritances in Zion, was likely mooted by Partridge's repentance, and that anyone claiming the title today 'manifests great ignorance.' Church materials treat the matter as settled by that statement.
cases.rationale: The 1905 statement is itself the interesting datum: for 73 years the verse sat open, spawning claimants, until the First Presidency resolved a canonized prophecy by newspaper reinterpretation — an authority move, not an exegesis members could have reached from the text. Not a lead argument; use it as supporting material on how the LDS canon handles unfulfilled prophecy, and it is directly useful in conversations touching fundamentalist offshoots, since nearly every splinter prophet has drafted this verse.

cases.title: The Snow couplet: taught for 150 years, minimized to the national press
cases.claim: 'As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be' — Lorenzo Snow's 1840 couplet, ratified by Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse (1844) and taught by prophets and manuals ever since (the Teachings of the Presidents: Lorenzo Snow manual features it). Yet when Time's Richard Ostling asked President Hinckley in 1997 whether God the Father was once a man, Hinckley answered: 'I don't know that we teach it. I don't know that we emphasize it... I understand the philosophical background behind it, but I don't know a lot about it.' He gave similar deflections to the San Francisco Chronicle ('that's more of a couplet than anything else'). The 2014 'Becoming Like God' essay robustly affirms the second half (human deification) while treating the first half — God's past as a man — with studied vagueness. So which is it: doctrine, speculation, or retired? The distinct issue here is institutional candor: what is taught inside is minimized outside.
bom: King Follett discourse (Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, pp. 345-46)

sources.name: Ronald Huggins, 'Lorenzo Snow's Couplet,' JETS 49/3 (2006)
Time interview text and context (Aug 4, 1997), compiled
Gospel Topics essay: 'Becoming Like God'
MRM on Richard Mouw and the couplet's status

cases.response: Apologists say Hinckley was answering narrowly — that the church does not emphasize or elaborate the doctrine because little has been revealed about it, not denying it; Hinckley told the next General Conference that news reports were 'incomplete.' The 'Becoming Like God' essay affirms that humans can become like God while noting scripture says little about God's past.
cases.rationale: Grade on the candor gap, not the doctrine (the doctrine itself is the exalted-man case, covered separately). The same church that publishes a prophet's manual featuring the couplet had its sitting prophet tell national media 'I don't know that we teach it.' Either the prophet didn't know his own doctrine or he was managing its public image — both are problems for a church claiming prophetic clarity. Huggins (JETS) traces the couplet's canonical-grade usage in church curricula, so 'we don't really teach it' is documentedly false. Conversationally strong: most members have sung 'If You Could Hie to Kolob' and learned the couplet; showing them Hinckley's answer lands.

cases.title: Evolution: prophets contradicted each other, then the church declared no position
cases.claim: The 1909 First Presidency statement 'The Origin of Man' declared Adam 'the first man of all men' and dismissed human evolution as 'theories of men.' The 1925 restatement quietly softened it. Apostles then split publicly for decades: Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie condemned evolution as heresy incompatible with the Fall, while James E. Talmage and B.H. Roberts accepted pre-Adamite life; today the church's official position is that it has no official position, and BYU teaches evolution as settled science. Meanwhile canonized texts still commit the church to no death before the Fall (2 Nephi 2:22, Alma 12:23-24; Moses 3:7 calls Adam 'the first flesh upon the earth') and D&C 77:6-7 to a 7,000-year temporal history — claims the church no longer defends but has never corrected. The question 'who was speaking as a prophet?' has no answer.

sources.name: Church History Topics: 'Organic Evolution'
'The Origin of Man' (1909), reprinted Ensign 2002
Dialogue: 'The Mormon Myth of Evil Evolution'
From the Desk: the 1909 and 1925 statements compared
Wikipedia: Mormon views on evolution

cases.response: The church's position is that the 1909 statement affirmed doctrines about humanity's divine origin, not a scientific mechanism; the 1910/1925 materials show openness; the church has no official position on evolution itself and 'leaves science to science.' BYU's board-approved evolution packet reflects this neutrality.
cases.rationale: Do not claim 'the church banned evolution' — it never quite did, and the neutrality framing has real support (the 1910 Christmas message, the BYU packet). The strong core is narrower and solid: apostles taught flatly contradictory positions on a factual question for 70 years while all claiming prophetic authority, and canonized no-death-before-the-Fall scripture remains uncorrected while functionally abandoned. Use it as a case study in how 'prophets, seers, and revelators' resolve empirical questions — they didn't; the scientists did, and the church followed. Corroboration, not your lead.

cases.title: 'Mormon' as a 'major victory for Satan' — after the church's own Mormon branding
cases.claim: In August-October 2018, President Russell M. Nelson declared that using 'Mormon' or 'LDS' for the church 'is a major victory for Satan' and an offense to Jesus, mandating the full name and triggering renames (Mormon Tabernacle Choir, LDS.org, mormon.org). Yet the church itself had just spent most of a decade and millions of dollars on the 'I'm a Mormon' ad campaign (2010-2018), the feature film 'Meet the Mormons' (2014), and official pages calling 'Mormon' an 'inoffensive nickname' — and Gordon B. Hinckley, as prophet, publicly embraced the term ('Mormon means more good,' Oct 1990 General Conference, responding to then-Elder Nelson's 1990 plea for the full name). Either the nickname aids Satan — indicting the prophets who ran the campaigns — or it doesn't, and 'victory for Satan' was rhetorical inflation delivered as prophetic correction. Nelson said the change was 'not a name change... it is a correction' commanded by the Lord.

sources.name: Salt Lake Tribune, Oct 7 2018: 'Members offend Jesus... President Nelson says'
Church News: 'President Russell M. Nelson: The Correct Name of the Church'
wasmormon.org: compilation of prior 'I'm a Mormon' / 'Meet the Mormons' usage
Fox News coverage of the 2018 policy

cases.response: Nelson taught that the Lord named the church in D&C 115:4 and that restoring the full name honors Christ; prior nickname campaigns were well-intentioned accommodations to public awareness, and prophets can receive updated direction — line upon line — without prior leaders being condemned.

responseSource.name: Nelson, 'The Correct Name of the Church' (Oct 2018 General Conference)

cases.rationale: A soft case doctrinally, but documented end to end from church sources and constantly live in conversation ('why can't we say Mormon anymore?'). Its value is as an accessible, low-stakes specimen of the pattern the bigger cases show: a prophet frames a reversal of his predecessors' publicly-taught position as timeless divine will, with 'Satan' attached to what the church itself did until that year. Use it as a gentle door-opener, not a centerpiece.

cases.title: Don't use: 'Mormons worship Joseph Smith'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Mormons worship Joseph Smith — they even sing hymns of praise to him.'

sources.name: Wikipedia: 'Praise to the Man'
MRM: 'Praise to the Man: Joseph Smith'
AskGramps: 'Doesn't Praise to the Man show we worship Joseph Smith?'

cases.response: False as stated. Latter-day Saints worship God the Father and Jesus Christ, not Smith; the church explicitly denies worshiping him, and members experience the accusation as an obvious misrepresentation. 'Praise to the Man' is veneration of a founder (with admittedly extravagant language — 'mingling with Gods'), not liturgical worship.
cases.rationale: Opening with 'you worship Joseph Smith' is factually wrong, instantly correctable, and marks you as someone who never met a Latter-day Saint. What's true and useful instead: everything distinctive in Mormonism rests epistemically on Smith's claims — Joseph Fielding Smith wrote 'Mormonism, as it is called, must stand or fall on the story of Joseph Smith' (Doctrines of Salvation 1:188). Say that: 'I know you worship Christ — but every distinctive doctrine depends on whether Joseph told the truth. Can we test that?' That is a door the member's own leaders opened.

cases.title: Don't use: 'The Mormon church owns Coca-Cola/Pepsi'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'The LDS church secretly owns Coca-Cola (or Pepsi) — banning caffeine while profiting from it.'
bom: D&C 89 (Word of Wisdom, the supposed irony hook)

sources.name: Snopes: 'Mormon Ownership of Coca-Cola'
FAIR: Rumor that the Church owns Coca-Cola
Faith Inspires: 'Do Mormons Own Pepsi?'

cases.response: Urban legend, flatly false. Snopes traces it to the 'delicious irony' appeal; no ownership stake has ever existed, and Ensign Peak's post-SEC-settlement 13F disclosures list no Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, or Keurig Dr Pepper holdings. The legend also rests on a second error — the church never banned caffeine (see the caffeine entry).
cases.rationale: Repeating a Snopes-debunked legend hands the member a free win and taints everything else you say. The documented finance story is far stronger than the legend: Ensign Peak's $100B+ concealed reserve and the 2023 SEC settlement (already on this site) are admitted, adjudicated fact. If church money is the topic, go there — 'the SEC fined your church for hiding $32 billion behind shell companies' needs no urban legend's help.

cases.title: Don't use: 'magic underwear' mockery
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Mormons wear magic underwear that protects them from harm.'

sources.name: Deseret News: church releases 'Sacred Temple Clothing' video (Oct 2014)
Church News: 'Church Produces Video on Sacred Nature and Purpose of Temple Garments'
Newsroom: 'Church Updates Temple Garment Video'

cases.response: The garments are real and the practice is documented (see the temple-garments case), but 'magic underwear' is mockery, not argument. The church's 2014 'Sacred Temple Clothing' video pre-empts exactly this line, comparing garments to the nun's habit, the prayer shawl, and the monk's robe, and calling the phrase 'inaccurate and offensive.' Folk beliefs about physical protection exist among members but are not official doctrine.
cases.rationale: Mocking someone's underclothing makes the Christian the aggressor, triggers the persecution frame the church has already built a video around, and forfeits the substantive point. The garments case worth making is about enforcement, not fabric: wearing is monitored via temple-recommend interview questions, and until recently women's garment norms were policed in detail — that's a question about religious control, and it survives being said respectfully. Ask, don't jeer: 'How did it feel to have an interview cover your underwear?'

cases.title: Don't use: inflated counts of Joseph Smith's wives
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Joseph Smith had 87 wives' (or 50+, or 'hundreds').

sources.name: Gospel Topics essay: 'Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo'
Wikipedia: List of Joseph Smith's wives
LDS Discussions: Polygamy and Polyandry in Nauvoo

cases.response: The documented count is about 30-40 — and that number is the church's own: the Gospel Topics essay says 'careful estimates put the number between 30 and 40,' citing Brian Hales; Todd Compton documents 33. Higher figures (Stanley Ivins once tallied 84) pad the list with unverifiable and posthumous sealings. Claiming 87 lets an apologist correct your arithmetic and walk away from the substance.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics: Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo

cases.rationale: Overclaiming is the one gift you can give FAIR on this topic. The church-admitted facts need no inflation: 30-40 wives, one aged 14 (Helen Mar Kimball, 'sealed months before her 15th birthday' per the essay), roughly a dozen already married to living husbands, and public denials throughout — every clause sourced to the church's own essay and covered by this site's existing polygamy cases. Say '30 to 40 — that's your church's number, footnoted to its own website,' and nothing can be rebutted.

cases.title: Don't use: 'Mormons still practice polygamy'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Mormons still practice polygamy today' (image: prairie dresses, plural households).

sources.name: Wikipedia: Second Manifesto (1904)
Gospel Topics essay: 'The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage'
Church History Topics: 'Plural Marriage after the Manifesto'

cases.response: False for the mainstream church: since the 1904 Second Manifesto, contracting or solemnizing a plural marriage gets you excommunicated, and today's practicing polygamists (FLDS, AUB, independents) are splinter groups the LDS church denounces. The prairie-dress image is FLDS, not LDS.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics: The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage

cases.rationale: Confusing LDS with FLDS is the fastest way to get politely dismissed. But drop the mortal-practice claim and the doctrinal one stands untouched, and it is covered on this site: D&C 132 remains canonized scripture, widowed men are sealed eternally to multiple wives today (Presidents Nelson and Oaks are both eternally sealed to two women), and the church's own history shows leaders secretly authorized plural marriages for 14 years after the 1890 Manifesto. Say: 'You're right, no one practices it now — so why is the revelation commanding it still in your scriptures, and why is eternal polygamy still live in your sealing policy?'

cases.title: Don't use: 'The White Horse Prophecy is LDS doctrine'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Mormon doctrine says a Mormon will ride in to save the Constitution when it hangs by a thread — the White Horse Prophecy — and Mormon politicians believe they're the one.'

sources.name: Church Newsroom statement, Jan 6 2010
Wikipedia: White Horse Prophecy
MRM: 'When the Constitution Hangs by a Thread'
From the Desk: What is the White Horse Prophecy?

cases.response: The church officially repudiated it in 2010: 'based on accounts that have not been substantiated by historical research and is not embraced as Church doctrine.' The full 'White Horse' text is a 1902 secondhand recollection of dubious provenance. Kernel to keep: the narrower 'Constitution will hang by a thread and the elders will save it' motif is genuinely and repeatedly attested in LDS leaders' teaching — Brigham Young and John Taylor taught it, and modern leaders (e.g., Ezra Taft Benson) invoked it.
cases.rationale: Cite the White Horse document as doctrine and the member quotes the 2010 repudiation back at you — conversation over. The defensible move is the kernel: the hang-by-a-thread teaching came from prophets' own mouths in documented sermons (Journal of Discourses 7:15 among others), which raises the same question with sources the church can't disown as folklore. Use the thread quotes; never lead with 'White Horse.'

cases.title: Don't use: 'Mormons can't have caffeine'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Mormons aren't allowed caffeine — no Coke, no Dr Pepper.'
bom: D&C 89:9 ('hot drinks are not for the body or belly')

sources.name: Fox 13: LDS church clarifies caffeine (Aug 2012 Newsroom response)
Newsweek: BYU begins selling caffeinated soda (2017)
FAIR: Word of Wisdom — cola drinks and caffeine

cases.response: False. The Word of Wisdom's 'hot drinks' has been officially interpreted as coffee and tea only; the church stated in 2012 that 'the Church does not prohibit the use of caffeine,' and BYU has sold caffeinated soda since 2017. Many faithful members drink Coke; caffeine appears nowhere in a temple-recommend interview.
cases.rationale: Getting this wrong signals you know Mormonism from playground rumor. The incoherence you were reaching for is sharper when stated accurately, and it's already on this site (the Word of Wisdom case): iced coffee is a temple-worthiness bar while a quad-shot energy drink is fine, the canonized text calls itself 'not by commandment or constraint' (D&C 89:2) yet became a salvation-gating test decades later, and 'hot drinks' meaning exactly coffee-and-tea is itself a post-hoc interpretation. Ask why the line falls where it does — don't misstate where the line is.

cases.title: Don't use (as phrased): 'Mormons get their own planet'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Mormons believe that if they're good enough, they each get their own planet when they die.'

sources.name: Gospel Topics essay: 'Becoming Like God'
Salt Lake Tribune coverage of the essay
MormonThink: response to 'Becoming Like God'
MRM: Gospel Topics essay 'Becoming Like God'

cases.response: The church's 2014 essay pre-loaded the rebuttal: exaltation is 'reduced in media to a cartoonish image of people receiving their own planets,' and a church FAQ answers 'No' to the planet question. Say 'own planet' and the member hands you the essay. The kernel, though, is strong and church-affirmed: exaltation means becoming gods (D&C 132:20 — 'then shall they be gods'), with eternal increase and participation in creation; past leaders taught it in exactly cosmic terms (Snow, Young, Kimball's 'we shall create worlds').
cases.rationale: This is the rare avoid-entry where the underlying doctrine is fully conceded — the error is purely in the packaging. 'Own planet' is South Park vocabulary the church has explicitly framed as caricature, so using it triggers the scripted deflection and skips the real conversation. Use the member's own words instead: 'Your scripture says the exalted “shall be gods” — D&C 132:20. Isaiah says “before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.” Can both be true?' The exaltation case on this site carries the full argument.

cases.title: Don't use: 'Joseph Smith was convicted of fraud in 1826'
cases.claim: Popular version: 'Joseph Smith was a convicted con man — a court convicted him of fraud in 1826, right before he found the plates.'

sources.name: Wikipedia: Joseph Smith and the criminal justice system
BYU Studies: 'Joseph Smith's 1826 Trial: The Legal Setting' (Madsen)
BYU Studies: 'Joseph Smith and the 1826 Trial: New Evidence and New Difficulties' (Hill)
Marquardt/UTLM: 'Joseph Smith's 1826 Trial — New Discoveries Prove Court Record Authentic'

cases.response: Overclaimed. The 1826 Bainbridge proceeding was real — Smith, age 20, was charged as a 'disorderly person' over paid 'glass looking' (Justice Neely's own fee bill labels him 'The Glass Looker') — but it was likely a preliminary examination, the surviving records are fragmentary and contradictory (the Pearsall account says 'guilty'; the fee/mittimus evidence points the other way), and scholars from Madsen (acquittal/discharge) to Vogel and Walters dispute the outcome. 'Convicted of fraud' states as fact what the documents cannot establish.
cases.rationale: Say 'convicted' and the apologist wins the exchange on the record's ambiguity — and the ambiguity is genuine, not spin. The core that needs no conviction: by the church's own Gospel Topics admission and Bushman's Rough Stone Rolling, Smith was a paid treasure-seer who hunted buried valuables by staring at a stone in his hat — the same stone, in the same hat, he then used to produce the Book of Mormon. The 1826 court documents corroborate that occupation ('The Glass Looker') regardless of verdict. Usage: corroboration, not your lead — lead with the church-admitted seer-stone facts (covered in the translation case) and let the 1826 record confirm the timeline.
